title: Hypertrophy Q&A #2
summary: NH answers viewer questions on direct ab work, HIT with one set to failure, judging whether volume and intensity are right, leg drive on bench, adjusting secondary movements across hard and easy weeks, oblique training, progression on secondary presses, and ring dips, pull-ups and ring rows for home training.
claims: Muscles that are prime movers in heavy compounds (quads, glutes, chest) don't need isolation; most others do
Even if compounds alone worked, you'd still need variations for more volume; any exercise biasing tonnage to one muscle is a form of isolation
Very new lifters can get by on squats alone
Abs need direct work: compounds brace them but don't stimulate them as needed; people saying otherwise lack six-packs or are on drugs
Skip planks; brace properly on compounds and add stretching ab movements like leg raises
Big forearms and arms require isolating them
The term 'high intensity training' is a problem: everyone training properly does high intensity at some point
High-volume programs tend to be junk volume and high-intensity programs too low in volume; you need both
One working set to failure is far too little for naturals
Every working set (not warm-ups) should be taken to failure, meaning failing within the rep-in-the-tank principle NH uses on strength work
NH distrusts studies claiming failure is unnecessary; he finds their parameters skewed toward their conclusion
How you feel during the workout and the next day means nothing for judging volume; listen to your body mainly for injury prevention
Your program is the boss; NH has often felt he couldn't hit his reps in warm-ups and been proved wrong
Soreness is not a good sign of activation or hypertrophy; it fades as recovery improves while you keep progressing
Changing programs to 'confuse the muscles' and get sore again is the best way to slow your gains
Volume and intensity are right as long as you progress (maximum recoverable volume); if it works, keep riding the wave
Lack of progression or regression means too little stimulus to carry you or too much (overreaching)
Too much volume and intensity is worse than too little, as long as progression stays constant
Leg drive matters for bodybuilders: it creates the arch, tucks the shoulders, raises the chest, shortens ROM and protects the rotator cuff
The less taxed the shoulder, the more you can damage the chest fibres and grow it
NH doesn't use clear-cut hard and easy weeks, which would be akin to deloads; volume and intensity fluctuate within the program
Strength work is the lighthouse: on a high-intensity bench day, the secondary press should be higher reps and lower intensity
On the second upper day of the week, take a set off the secondary movement to account for accumulated fatigue
On hard weeks, skip secondary movements when retraining an area; if choosing, keeping the secondary movement preserves tonnage better than keeping strength work
Sacrificial approach: day 1 strength work only at high volume and intensity, day 2 high-intensity low-volume strength work plus the secondary movement
Benching 150 lb for 10 at 150 lb bodyweight is not horrible; a light lifter shouldn't focus on strength, and if skinny-fat should recomp
NH has big obliques from squats and deadlifts and never isolated them; anything requiring core rigidity builds them
NH has never seen big biceps or long head triceps without isolation, but naturally big obliques are frequent
For obliques without twisting, try hanging leg raises to the side or lying leg raises held vertical and slowly lowered side to side for a stretch
A back-off set replicates the main movement (e.g. bench 3x5 then AMRAP); a different style like close-grip is a variation, not a back-off set
Don't try to progress both the main lift and its secondary variation at once; letting one stall is a deliberate 'tonnage sacrifice', not a plateau
You can also hold strength tonnage steady and push progression on the secondary movement; progression is not driven by strength work alone
Main and secondary lifts feed each other, the heavier more so; technical limits like the front rack can block carryover
If secondary press reps hold steady while main bench reps rise, you're getting stronger since you enter the secondary set more fatigued
Dips are just as valid as bench press and may be better because they give a greater pec and shoulder stretch
The bar limiting bench ROM is a blessing that prevents shoulder injuries; dips need precise ROM control and lack safeties, and ring dips double the risk
Keep weighted ring dips at 6-10 reps, not 3-5, and if you won't keep doing dips after lockdown, stick to bodyweight
Pull-ups, ideally weighted, are all you need for lats and vertical pulling
Ring rows are great but hard to load (a 10 kg vest isn't enough), which is why NH does seal rows
Pull-ups plus ring rows leave rear delts and upper traps short; shrugs matter
Be wary of minimalist exercise selection; if your development is limited, add exercises

legs vertical, lower slowly to each side
great pec stretch but very risky for shoulders
